details:
**Lysistrata (sex strike to end the Peloponnesian War)**
Aristophanes' most famous play (411 BCE), and the most common giveaway for him. The title heroine persuades the women of Athens and Sparta to withhold sex from their husbands until the men make peace and end the Peloponnesian War.

**"Brekekekex koax koax"**
The croaking refrain of the frog chorus in The Frogs, sung as Dionysus rows across the underworld lake Acheron. The frogs' endless chanting irritates Dionysus, and the line is one of the most frequent clues for the playwright.

**The Thinkery (Phrontisterion)**
The school of Socrates in The Clouds. The debt-ridden old farmer Strepsiades enrolls (and later sends his son Pheidippides) there to learn clever arguments for escaping his creditors; at the end, enraged, he burns the Thinkery down.

**Strepsiades and Pheidippides**
The father and son of The Clouds. Strepsiades' debts come from his son's love of horses; after his schooling, Pheidippides beats his father and argues that doing so is morally justified, which drives Strepsiades to burn the school.

**Socrates in a basket**
In The Clouds, Socrates first appears suspended in a basket in the air, claiming he must hang aloft to contemplate the heavens. The play also shows his students measuring how far a flea can jump by dipping its feet in wax and explaining that a gnat buzzes through its rear end.

**Right Logic vs. Wrong Logic**
The two personified arguments (also translated Just and Unjust Argument, or Stronger and Weaker) that debate in The Clouds. Wrong Logic wins, satirizing the sophists who taught people to make the weaker argument defeat the stronger.

**Cloud-cuckoo-land (Nephelokokkygia)**
The city in the sky built by the birds in The Birds. Two Athenians, Pisthetaerus and Euelpides, leave Athens, seek out the Hoopoe (a former man named Tereus), and persuade the birds to build a city between heaven and earth that cuts the gods off from human sacrifices.

**Philocleon and the dog trial (The Wasps)**
In The Wasps, the old man Philocleon is addicted to serving on juries, so his son Bdelycleon locks him in the house and sets up a mock court at home. There a dog resembling Cleon accuses another dog of stealing a Sicilian cheese, with kitchen utensils such as a cheese grater and a pestle as witnesses; the play inspired Racine's comedy Les Plaideurs.

**Cleon**
The Athenian demagogue and war hawk whom Aristophanes repeatedly attacked. Cleon took credit for the victory over Sparta at Sphacteria (Pylos) and prosecuted Aristophanes over his lost play The Babylonians; Aristophanes answered by satirizing him in The Knights and The Wasps, whose names Philocleon ("Cleon-lover") and Bdelycleon ("Cleon-loather") mock him.

**The Knights and the sausage-seller**
In The Knights, a stolen oracle prophesies that the tanner (Paphlagon, a stand-in for Cleon) will be overthrown by a sausage-seller. The sausage-seller, Agoracritus, beats Cleon in a series of contests for the favor of the old man Demos, who personifies the Athenian people.

**Dionysus and Xanthias in the underworld (The Frogs)**
In The Frogs, the bumbling god Dionysus travels to Hades to bring back the tragedian Euripides. He disguises himself as Heracles and repeatedly swaps clothes with his slave Xanthias, makes Xanthias walk around the lake while he takes Charon's boat, and Xanthias gets blamed for Heracles' earlier theft of Cerberus.

**Aeschylus vs. Euripides and the weighing of verses**
The poetry contest that closes The Frogs. Lines from each tragedian are weighed on a scale, and Aeschylus mocks Euripides' prologues by repeatedly ending them with "lost his little oil flask"; Aeschylus is judged the best tragic poet and brought back to life instead of Euripides.

**Reconciliation, the naked handmaid**
A personification who appears in Lysistrata (sometimes translated as Peace). The negotiators for Athens and Sparta are distracted by her naked body and map their territorial demands onto it as the peace treaty is drawn up.

**Lysistrata's wool metaphor and the Commissioner**
In Lysistrata, the heroine tells the Commissioner (Magistrate) that the city should be managed like wool: washed, carded of its parasites, and woven into a cloak for the people. The women dress the Commissioner as a woman and later as a corpse; the play also features the women seizing the Acropolis treasury, old men who try to burn them out and are doused with water, and Myrrhine teasing her husband Kinesias.

**Peace and Trygaeus' dung beetle**
In Peace, the farmer Trygaeus flies to heaven on a giant dung beetle and discovers the gods have left, leaving War in charge, who has buried the goddess Peace in a cave. He rallies the Greeks to free her and marries her attendant Harvest (Opora); the play opens with slaves kneading dung to feed the beetle.
